parts.note: not the idiom for arrogance but literally a horse that travels high up, the winged steed of Greek myth

explanation.walkthrough: 'High horse' reads as the phrase for haughty behaviour; here it is simply a horse that flies.
explanation.definitionFit: The winged steed of Greek legend soared through the sky, so it is a horse that is literally high.

clue.text: A light blow under mine — makes my heart go thus?

indicators.note: in a down clue, the piece under another is written below it, so it follows

parts.note: a pit is a coal mine
a pat is a gentle tap

explanation.surface: A soft tap below a mine, and a fluttering heart.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'under' means placed after. The definition is the light rapid sound a heart makes when it flutters with excitement.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick light tapping sound, like a heart beating fast with excitement.

clue.text: They look ugly but can be gushing

definitions.text: They look ugly but can be gushing

parts.words: They look ugly but can be gushing
parts.note: sounds like unattractive people who are effusive, but means grotesque carved spouts that pour out rainwater

explanation.surface: Unattractive people who nonetheless turn out effusive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gushing' looks like effusive praise; these carved stone figures literally gush rainwater from church gutters.
explanation.definitionFit: Grotesque carved spouts on churches throw rainwater clear of the walls.

clue.text: Just the thing for writing fashion articles ?

definitions.text: Just the thing for writing fashion articles

parts.words: Just the thing for writing fashion articles
parts.note: sounds like a fashion journalist's skill, but combines an old writing instrument with the word for fashion

explanation.surface: Advice on what suits a journalist covering the clothing pages.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is both a pointed writing implement (a stylus) and fashion; 'articles' suggests magazine pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means fashion or flair, and also an old pointed implement for writing on wax tablets.

clue.text: A display of grit in the desert

definitions.text: A display of grit in the desert

parts.words: A display of grit in the desert
parts.note: grit sounds like courage, but here it is literal: wind-driven particles flying in the desert

explanation.surface: Showing courage under hard conditions in a wilderness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grit' means courage on the surface, but is literal sand blown about by a desert storm.
explanation.definitionFit: A desert gale whips up clouds of fine particles, filling the air with grit.

parts.note: someone who is not ardent is lukewarm or mild
Red is the familiar label for a Communist

explanation.surface: A woman described as a half-hearted member of the Communist Party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'she' defines a woman's name: a mild Red is a Communist who is no ardent one.
explanation.definitionFit: A female given name, so it can stand for any particular woman referred to as she.

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of the next word could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: The estate of an ancient nobleman, perhaps from Roman times.
explanation.definitionFit: A feudal estate held by a lord in medieval England.

clue.text: But he doesn't recite poems in church

definitions.text: But he doesn't recite poems in church

parts.words: But he doesn't recite poems in church
parts.note: lays are old poems, so one reading lays would recite poems; instead this is a non-clergy person reading lessons in church

explanation.surface: A churchgoer who does not perform verse at services.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'lay' is a ballad or poem, so a lay reader sounds like a poetry reciter; in fact lay means not ordained.
explanation.definitionFit: A layman licensed to conduct parts of church services without being ordained.

parts.note: chicken-hearted means cowardly, but read literally it is the hens themselves, who need a perch

explanation.walkthrough: 'Chicken-hearted' suggests cowards needing moral support; it is literally a perch for chickens.
explanation.definitionFit: A perch on which hens and other birds settle to sleep.

clue.text: Sort Dad out of these old codgers

indicators.note: out means put out of order, so the letters of the two words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: Sorting out Dad, from among a group of elderly men.
explanation.definitionFit: Elderly people grown feeble-minded, a disparaging word for old men in their decline.

definitions.meaning: to linger or delay, an old word for staying put
the adjective for something coated in or like pitch, dark and sticky

explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to linger or stay; as an adjective it describes something smeared with pitch, hence black.

clue.text: She has her own kids to look after

definitions.text: She has her own kids to look after

parts.words: She has her own kids to look after
parts.note: sounds like a babysitter or mother, but kids are young goats and the carer is a female goat

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a childminder; 'kids' means young goats, and the female goat looks after her own.
explanation.definitionFit: A female goat nurses her young, which are called kids.

definitions.meaning: ... Challenger is the explorer-scientist in Arthur Conan Doyle's The Lost World
an academic who holds a university chair, the senior teaching post

explanation.walkthrough: 'Challenger' looks like a rival in a contest; it is Conan Doyle's character, who bears the academic title.
explanation.definitionFit: Conan Doyle's hero carries this title, and the holder of a university chair is given it.

parts.note: a consuming passion sounds like an obsession, but read literally it is a fondness for consuming, i.e. food

explanation.walkthrough: 'Consuming passion' is taken literally: a passion for consuming food.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who consumes food, especially with relish, is described by this word.

parts.note: groundwork is literal: working the ground, ploughing the soil before planting the produce of 23 down

explanation.surface: Someone prepares the way for something else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groundwork' usually means preparation; here it is literally working the soil, and 23 down is the farm produce grown there.
explanation.definitionFit: A farmer cultivates and turns the soil to prepare for planting harvests.

indicators.note: in places one word within another

parts.note: the answer to 26 across, the platform Jaques speaks of
still as an adverb means even, as in still better

explanation.surface: A recently built town still features in a theatrical show.
explanation.walkthrough: '26' points to the answer of 26 across. Stevenage, in Hertfordshire, was Britain's first post-war new town.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hertfordshire town designated in 1946 as the first of Britain's planned post-war towns.

clue.text: Roads one can repair for the islanders

indicators.note: to repair is to rebuild, so the letters of the words before it are put together anew

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Councils fixing roads for the people living on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: ROADS + I (one) + CAN, rearranged as 'repair' asks, gives the islanders of Orkney.
explanation.definitionFit: The people of Orkney, the archipelago off northern Scotland, are known by this name.

clue.text: Studies three points with us to reach agreement

parts.note: to con is to study or learn by heart, so studies gives cons
E, N and S are three compass points
taken as written

explanation.surface: A scholar studies three points with colleagues to reach a shared view.
explanation.walkthrough: CON is an old word for study; E, N and S are compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: General agreement among a group, a shared opinion.

parts.note: stately homes suggests grand country houses, but read as homes in the States it describes a nation's people

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stately homes' are British country mansions; read as 'States-ly' homes they belong to the people of the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Citizens of the United States, whose homeland is the States.

parts.note: suggests someone awaiting arrest or a reservation, but refers to a title character of a novel whose surname is Ready

explanation.walkthrough: Masterman Ready is a Victorian children's novel by Captain Marryat: the character 'Ready' is put in a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Marryat's novel Masterman Ready names its seaman hero, whose first name is this and surname is Ready.

parts.note: largely looks like mostly, but hints at the creature's size: a huge woolly beast long since died out

explanation.walkthrough: 'Largely' seems to mean 'mostly'; it hints that the beast's name also means huge.
explanation.definitionFit: An extinct woolly elephant of the Ice Age, whose name also means huge.

clue.text: Unsuitable dances for those going steady?

definitions.text: Unsuitable dances for those going steady?

parts.words: Unsuitable dances for those going steady
parts.note: going steady sounds like a couple's romance, but means walking steadily; the dance word also means staggers

explanation.walkthrough: The word is both lively Scottish dances and staggering about, which no steady walker does.
explanation.definitionFit: Lively Scottish and Irish dances share their name with the verb for staggering drunkenly.

clue.text: Where has —— to buy illicit liquor ?

definitions.text: Where has —— to buy illicit liquor

parts.words: Where has —— to buy illicit liquor
parts.note: the blank is filled by two words, a pronoun and a past participle, making a question about where a woman went; together they name an unlicensed drinking den

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap with SHE BEEN: 'Where has she been?' A shebeen is an unlicensed Irish or Scottish drinking house.
explanation.definitionFit: An unlicensed bar selling illicit alcohol, a word from Ireland and Scotland.

clue.text: Big American brute, but sounds sweet

indicators.note: the word sounds tells us to swap the dessert for a word pronounced the same way

parts.note: a mousse is a light whipped dessert, a sweet

explanation.surface: A large American thug who is surprisingly sweet-voiced.
explanation.definitionFit: North America's largest deer, a huge beast also called an elk in Europe.

parts.note: sounds like long-awaited post arriving, but means the final character of the Greek alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: 'A letter at last!' sounds like relief at the post; it is the last letter of the Greek alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The final character of the Greek alphabet, hence a symbol of the end.

clue.text: But still a part of dear old London !

definitions.text: But still a part of dear old London

parts.words: But still a part of dear old London
parts.note: dear means costly, so the opposite of dear is still part of London: a street name built on the word for inexpensive

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dear old London' is affectionate, but 'dear' means costly: the City street with 'cheap' in its name is the opposite, yet still part of London.
explanation.definitionFit: A historic street in the City of London, once its main market, whose name begins with the word for inexpensive.

parts.note: short cuts sound like quicker routes, but means clipping or harvesting close on a farm

explanation.walkthrough: The word means both harvests and closely clipped haircuts or trimmings.
explanation.definitionFit: Farm harvests share their name with close trims, such as a cropped haircut.

parts.note: brilliant seems to praise a mimic, but refers to a diamond-cut gem faked in glass

explanation.walkthrough: 'Brilliant' is a cut of diamond; the imitation is the hard glass used for fake jewellery.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard glass used to make fake gems that imitate a diamond.

clue.text: Those after inside information in the theatre ?

definitions.text: Those after inside information in the theatre

parts.words: Those after inside information in the theatre
parts.note: sounds like spies or gossips at a play, but the theatre is the operating theatre and the inside is the body

explanation.walkthrough: The theatre is the operating theatre, and the 'inside information' is the patient's insides.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgeons who carry out operations are so called, and they work in operating theatres.

parts.note: refers to the speech by Jaques in Shakespeare's As You Like It, which says all the world is a platform for players

explanation.walkthrough: Jaques in Shakespeare's As You Like It says 'All the world's a stage'.
explanation.definitionFit: The platform for actors in a theatre, which Jaques compares to the whole world.

parts.note: Faith looks like an old oath and let well alone like leaving things be; it means those using faith alone to make people well

explanation.walkthrough: 'Faith' reads like an exclamation; it means faith healing, practitioners who make the sick well by faith alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Faith healers cure by belief rather than medicine, restoring people to health.

clue.text: Relative who knows what to do with the accelerator?

definitions.text: Relative who knows what to do with the accelerator?

parts.words: Relative who knows what to do with the accelerator
parts.note: a family member by remarriage whose title, split in two, describes pressing a pedal with the foot

explanation.walkthrough: Split as STEPS ON, the relation describes what a driver does to the accelerator pedal.
explanation.definitionFit: A wife's or husband's son from an earlier marriage is a relation by remarriage.
